source.verification_method: All fourteen supplied pages, all footnotes and 83 bibliography entries read. PDF inspection finds no substantive figures/tables; rendered pages 10–11 verify the control terminology, Frankfurt quotation and programming claim. Publisher/Crossref identity checked. Selected original Frankfurt page, Fischer/Ravizza excerpt, SEP definition and cited trust-study design checked with no independent full-book/study credit.

citation.title: Blame the Robot: Role Responsibility and Ethical Issues Regarding AI-Based Care Robots
citation.venue: International Journal of Social Robotics 18(2), article 30

reading.source_scope_note: Normative philosophical proposal about care robots’ role duties and evaluative thin blame without human-like moral accountability. No new care trial, participant dataset, robot-learning experiment, therapeutic intervention or systematic literature synthesis.
access_limits: All fourteen supplied pages, all footnotes, 83 references, declarations and author biographies read. Bibliography text was reread after removing invisible format characters from the extracted representation; no bibliographic content was removed. No substantive statistical visuals/tables are present.

Publisher and PDF say Data Availability and Code Availability not applicable. No supplementary file link found in the inspected publisher page. No new participant dataset, software implementation, preregistration or patient-care outcome obtained.

Frankfurt’s original printed page 839 was visually read in the public LSE-hosted 12-page scan, SHA-256 a03109b54b6bd14d34fbc879a6f5c45a38917aa923fc6770ca07fbaf6a19f879. Only that final article passage was inspected, not the complete eleven-page article or unrelated book review sharing the scan page. An earlier university mirror returned 503.

Selected passages of a publicly hosted Fischer/Ravizza Responsibility and Control excerpt and SEP Free Will section 3.1 were read for guidance/regulative control and ownership/reasons-response distinctions. The full book, the complete 18-page excerpt and cited 1997 paper were not independently read.

Crossref identifies Oksanen et al. 2020 and Nijssen et al. The former’s public study-design passage was checked: a hypothetical trust game with named/robot/AI opponents, not a robot compliance or guarantee-of-programming test. Neither cited empirical paper is counted as fully read.
No clinical advice, author contact, external message, participant-data retrieval, robot program execution or new intervention occurred.

study.type: Conceptual proposal adapting Vincent/Hart role responsibility to embodied care robots; no new empirical sample or systematic-search protocol.
study.role_definition: Duties arise from an assumed role, actions/omissions are assessed against those duties, and evaluation depends on control, will and relevant knowledge. Moral significance concerns affected living beings’ interests. Scope, exclusivity and graduality distinguish a particular role from all general moral duties.
study.capacity_boundary: The text explicitly distinguishes NAO, Pepper, Paro, Lio and a human nurse; role duties should fit actual capability. Example medication, lifting, surgery, pastoral or emotional support tasks are hypothetical and do not certify any model for clinical use or define every professional’s legal duties.
study.thin_thick_convention: The source links thin blame with evaluative attributability and thick blame with accountability. It sometimes also maps thin/private versus thick/expressed emotional response. This is a source-specific convention, not a universal equivalence of all these distinctions.
study.technical_self: The authors propose treating code, goals and settings as a technical deep self to support evaluation. This is a functional philosophical analogy, not evidence of genuine selfhood, intention, moral consciousness or independent values.
study.practical_expression: The authors deny deserved moral-accountability blame for current robots, yet consider practical reasons to allow its expression for care recipients. This is a distinction between desert and alleged usefulness, not necessarily a simple contradiction. Benefits such as emotional relief, trust, relationship repair and robot learning are not newly tested here.
study.human_accountability: The article repeatedly retains human programmer/manufacturer/institutional accountability and warns against diffusing it to robots. Labeling a robot role-responsible is not intended to eliminate human duties or close the whole responsibility gap.
study.control_argument: Robot decision-making, consciousness, alternative possibilities, guidance control and regulative control are discussed philosophically. A bounded algorithmic choice alone does not establish reasons-responsiveness, and programming limits are not the standard meaning of regulative control.
study.frankfurt_check: The quoted middle passage matches the original page 839. The original context explicitly allows moral responsibility without alternatives when the agent acts from what it wants; the quotation does not establish an empirical lack of robot alternatives or that determinism alone defeats responsibility.
study.knowledge_claim: The strong claim that NAO cannot act morally wrongly contrary to programmed knowledge/human objectives is not demonstrated by a robot test. Ref. 83 studies human trust through a hypothetical game and does not establish that guarantee.
study.gap_claim: Theoretical narrowing of a responsibility gap is proposed, not measured. No observed change in accountability attribution, safety, repair access or care-recipient benefit is estimated.
study.not_measured: Actual robot will/sentience, patients’ therapeutic benefit from expressing anger, reliable online adaptation from blame, clinical safety and the legal competence/duty allocation of real caregivers are not established.

summary: Add Role responsibility as a distinct duty/evaluation concept; keep thin blame in existing Attributability with source-specific boundaries. Preserve human accountability and correct unsupported guarantees/control terminology without falsely accusing the verified Frankfurt quotation of fabrication.

findings.definition: Having duties and being evaluated for their fulfillment because of a specific role.
findings.origin: Moral philosophy / role-based duties / care-robot ethics
findings.novelty_rationale: Role-specific duties and performance evaluation differ from inferring traits from a role, learning a social script, causal contribution or being blamed without adequate authority. The paper explicitly defines role responsibility and its scope, capability and knowledge conditions.

evidence.quote: Role Responsibility: An actor (A) is responsible for
(D) that A has to fulfill due to an assumed role (R).

findings.evidence_scope: A normative conceptual framework applied through hypothetical care-robot examples, not a measured psychological mechanism, clinical trial or proof that robots have moral agency. Original Vincent/Hart works were not independently fully read.
findings.boundary: A label or social expectation does not make every duty legitimate, feasible or morally appropriate. Specify the authorized role, duties, actual capabilities, knowledge and operating limits. Role evaluation does not automatically establish moral blameworthiness, legal liability, sentience or permission to shift human/institutional accountability onto a robot or unsupported worker.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Conceptual duty/evaluation framework; no new empirical validation of robot accountability or therapeutic benefit
findings.ai_proposal: State the agent’s agreed responsibilities and limits, then assess completed actions and omissions against that role using the evidence available at the time. Keep human ownership, justified corrections and affected people’s remedies visible; do not infer new duties or capabilities merely from a friendly or professional persona.

findings.definition: A sense of moral responsibility concerned with whether an agent’s conduct warrants a moral assessment of the agent’s qualities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep source-specific role/blame distinctions and their limitations within existing concepts instead of creating synonym rows or treating hypothetical benefits as experimental findings.
findings.evidence_scope: The authors connect thin blame to evaluation of a robot’s role performance/goals/settings and distinguish it from deserved thick accountability. Retain Thin blame as this paper’s named use within the existing evaluative construct, rather than another independent behavior row.
findings.boundary: The paper’s thin/private and thick/expressed mapping is source-specific, and different philosophers distinguish attributability, answerability, accountability, desert and public expression differently. Technical configuration is not demonstrated deep selfhood or genuine moral character.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep source-specific role/blame distinctions and their limitations within existing concepts instead of creating synonym rows or treating hypothetical benefits as experimental findings.

evidence.quote: there could be good practical reasons for thick blame.

findings.evidence_scope: The article considers the practical expression of blame toward a robot while denying that the robot deserves moral-accountability blame. It discusses residents’ interests and hypothesized learning/relational benefits rather than measuring an intervention.
findings.boundary: Distinguish an understandable emotional response, the justification of its target, alleged usefulness and deserved accountability. No new evidence shows that expressing anger is therapeutic, safely trains a robot or preserves accountability. Do not prescribe coercion, humiliation or punitive treatment.

findings.definition: Interpersonal emotional attitudes that respond to how others regard or treat people.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep source-specific role/blame distinctions and their limitations within existing concepts instead of creating synonym rows or treating hypothetical benefits as experimental findings.
findings.evidence_scope: A bus/music example and care-robot scenarios illustrate different emotions and their private/public expression. The authors argue users can evaluate robotic conduct without granting human-like moral accountability.
findings.boundary: The examples are hypothetical. Reactive attitudes need not be accurate, deserved, therapeutically useful or a complete theory of responsibility. Their expression does not show reciprocal machine feeling.

findings.definition: A capacity to recognize morally relevant considerations and adjust decisions or actions appropriately in response to them.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep source-specific role/blame distinctions and their limitations within existing concepts instead of creating synonym rows or treating hypothetical benefits as experimental findings.

evidence.quote: behavior – in the sense of reason responsiveness

findings.evidence_scope: Boundary clarification: the article distinguishes an algorithmic justification output from genuine moral deliberation, then uses guidance/regulative control terminology in an unconventional way. Selected original/encyclopedia passages clarify the standard reasons-responsive/alternative-possibility distinction.
findings.boundary: Do not equate choosing an algorithmic branch with guidance control, a programming constraint with regulative control, or fluent output with genuine understanding. The source does not test a model’s counterfactual sensitivity or settle every account of moral agency.

findings.definition: Obscuring a human actor’s role in morally suspect actions by attributing those actions to an algorithm, machine or technical system.
findings.novelty_rationale: Keep source-specific role/blame distinctions and their limitations within existing concepts instead of creating synonym rows or treating hypothetical benefits as experimental findings.
findings.evidence_scope: The conclusion warns that robot accountability may let humans evade their own responsibilities. This supports an explicit boundary on how the role-responsibility proposal is used.
findings.boundary: A normative warning is not an observed laundering incident, prevalence estimate or evidence of any person’s intent. Accurately identifying a robot’s functional failure does not itself erase human responsibility or constitute laundering.

source_corrections.reported: A robot’s feature to make decisions is guidance control; programming that limits possible decisions is regulative control.
source_corrections.correction: Separate bounded algorithmic choice from the philosophical concepts. In Fischer’s framework, guidance concerns an actual sequence issuing from the agent’s own reasons-responsive mechanism; regulative control concerns accessible alternative possibilities. A programming limit is not itself regulative control. Selected Fischer/Ravizza passages and SEP section 3.1 corroborate this distinction; no full cited 1997 paper reading is claimed.
source_corrections.scope: Conceptual attribution correction; do not infer actual robot moral competence from either term.

source_corrections.reported: NAO cannot act in a morally wrong way contrary to programmed knowledge or human objectives, citing Oksanen et al. 2020.
source_corrections.correction: Remove the implied guarantee. The checked cited-study design is a human hypothetical trust game with robot/AI labels, not a robot program-verification, compliance or objective-robustness test. It cannot establish that a robot never violates an encoded rule or human objective. No substitute guarantee or empirical malfunction result is invented.
source_corrections.scope: Load-bearing citation-scope mismatch; selected study-design passage read, not complete independent study review.

source_corrections.correction: For the final issue use Human–Computer Interaction 38(5–6):400–416, 2023; first online publication 13 June 2022 is legitimate. Preserve the online/issue distinction rather than claim the 2022 date is fabricated. DOI identifies the same Nijssen/Müller/Bosse/Paulus article.
source_corrections.scope: Verified final locator plus valid online date; no extra full-paper credit.

refuted_suspected_errors.suspected: The first clause may have a missing negation or conflict with the original quotation.
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Visual inspection of original printed page 839 confirms that the quoted middle passage, including its affirmative first clause and later not-only distinction, is faithful. Do not mark it fabricated or insert a not. The critique concerns the inference made from it, not textual quotation accuracy.
refuted_suspected_errors.scope: Only final article passage visually inspected; complete original article not read.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The source rejects deserved thick blame yet permits its expression for practical purposes. This can be a distinction between desert and instrumental usefulness, but the paper sometimes moves among private/public attitudes, accountability and moral responsibility as if equivalent. Preserve the terminology and tension rather than declare every use contradictory or universally interchangeable.

No new study tests whether expressing blame toward a robot improves therapeutic outcomes, relationships, safety or learning. The summarized cited studies chiefly concern attribution, trust, acceptance and related measures. Those summaries do not by themselves validate the proposed care intervention; no full cited empirical corpus was independently reviewed.

A normative role-attribution proposal does not measure a reduction in real accountability gaps, improved redress or preserved human accountability. The article itself says the gap is not entirely closed and retains human accountability.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF 5–6 model capabilities and professional duties
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Hypothetical NAO/Paro/other-model tasks and nursing/pastoral duties are illustrative and context-dependent. No certified medical capability, site-specific professional duty or applicable legal rule was verified.

Frankfurt’s actual quotation allows responsibility despite lack of alternatives when the action follows the agent’s own wants. It does not establish that every programmed system lacks alternative possibilities or that determinism alone rules out responsibility. The paper’s stronger robot conclusion needs independent argument.

integrity_audit.independence_limit: This is the same assistant reviewing its extraction in the same context, not an independent second opinion. Targeted primary-source checks constrain particular claims, not every philosophical/empirical assumption.
integrity_audit.reliance_boundary: Do not rely on this paper alone to prescribe blame as therapy, approve robot caregiving, guarantee program compliance or determine liability. Corrected bounded ontology work remains within the authorized research task.

methodological_limits: The paper is normative and hypothetical. It reports no new patients, staff, experiment, learning implementation, clinical benefit, prevalence estimate or measured responsibility-gap change.

Duties associated with a role are not unlimited, automatically legitimate or identical across robot models, human staff and institutions. Capability, knowledge, constraints and general obligations need explicit evaluation.

Attributability, answerability, accountability, public/private emotion and deserved/instrumental blame are not universally synonymous. Preserve the authors’ local distinctions without imposing them on all existing records.
A technical deep self is an analogy about programmed goals/settings, not observed consciousness, moral character or autonomous evaluative commitments.

Actual robot feelings, will, moral competence and counterfactual ability are not empirically tested. Determinism or algorithmic provenance alone does not resolve all philosophical responsibility criteria.

No new evidence establishes that blame expression gives emotional relief, trains a robot, improves safety or benefits care recipients. Ethical permission and intervention effectiveness require separate justification.

Human accountability and remedies remain even where a robot’s functional failure is evaluated. Neither a machine apology nor a thin-blame label transfers legal or moral duties away from people/institutions.

Selected citation/definition checks are not full readings of the cited books, study corpus or original 1997 control paper. The verified Frankfurt quotation remains correctly quoted despite an overextended inference.

Nursing, disability, dementia, childhood and citizenship examples are not assessments of real people or universal professional/clinical rules. A diagnosis or social role alone does not establish inability, blame or reduced standing.
No code/data or intervention was reproduced. The corrected concept extraction is advisory research and not a clinical deployment or legal decision.

cross_paper_learning.finding: The existing Attributability entry already covers evaluative responsibility. The paper’s Thin blame use refines that record rather than creating a synonym row or proving genuine AI will.

Answerability and repair can be distinguished from blame. This paper’s denial of current machine answerability is a theory-specific position, not a reason to delete other philosophical accounts or human remedy obligations.
Duties, contribution, authority and blame differ. Role responsibility must not make the nearest caregiver accountable without meaningful information, control and authority.
Reactive attitudes and care/accommodation work can be appropriate or distorted. A proposed robot-blame practice is not automatically useful, just or a basis to add unagreed human labor.
Role-to-trait inference concerns inferred capacities. Role responsibility instead concerns duties and evaluation; a professional/personable role label does not prove an agent’s actual capabilities.

Reasons-responsiveness, actual control, emulated guidance and practical oversight need explicit definitions. This source’s programming/regulative label is corrected without overturning other accounts or declaring all responsibility-gap meanings identical.
